chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 491 to 500, Peyanar's mullai decade on the arrival (வரவுச் சிறப்புரைத்த பத்து): the man back from war or work tells the woman he hurried home with the rains, and the friend says the season and her beauty have returned together because he came.

thinai_evidence.note: the man returns as the rains arrive, the waiting of mullai ended

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the first-person verb of arrival makes the returned man the speaker, addressing the woman

491.reading: The returned man tells the woman that when the season met the rains he suffered without pause, and with a heart that ached again and again he has hurried back so that her beauty may return.
491.nuance: The decade's frame is the arrival, but this first poem gives the man's side of the waiting: the pain of the season was his too, and the purpose of his haste is her beauty (ஏர்), not his own relief.

thinai_evidence.note: peacock, mullai flower and deer of the rainy scrub

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the opening mullai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the first-person verb of arrival makes the returned man the speaker, addressing the woman

492.reading: The man tells the woman that with the peacock dancing like her, the mullai opening with the scent of her forehead and the deer gazing startled as she does, he came thinking of her, faster even than the rain clouds.
492.nuance: The comparisons run backward: she is the standard and the season's creatures are likened to her (நின்னே போலும் மஞ்ஞை), so every sign of the rains was, for him, a likeness of her. 'Faster than the rains' claims he beat the deadline the season sets.

thinai_evidence.note: the doe with her fawn as the rains begin

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the first-person verb of arrival makes the returned man the speaker, addressing the woman

493.reading: The man tells the woman that the rains began just as he came, thinking of her of the well-shaped forearm: the bulls grew fierce, the thunder roared back at them, and the lovely doe roamed bewildered with her fawn.
493.nuance: The line puns on ஏறு, bull and thunder, setting the beasts' rut against the sky's answer. The doe that wanders with her fawn is not given an act that maps onto the lovers, so it is left as scene, though a reader may hear the waiting mother in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the fragrant scrubland with its mullai in flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the first-person verb of arrival makes the returned man the speaker, addressing the woman

494.reading: The man tells the woman that with bees sucking pollen, frogs croaking their fill and the mullai of the cool fragrant scrub in flower, the season has turned to delight: he has accomplished what she needed, so let her grief now end.
494.nuance: நின் குறை வாய்த்தனம் may mean he has done what she lacked (come home in time) or that he finished the task for her sake; either way the poem makes the season's pleasure conditional on his return.

thinai_evidence.note: the red-soil scrub that has lost its loneliness

comparisons.tenor: the woman's teeth, sharp as sprouts

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the first-person verb of arrival makes the returned man the speaker, addressing the woman

495.reading: The man tells the woman that the scrub of red earth, strewn with many flowers, has lost its loneliness and turned sweet because he has come, with a heart that wept each time he thought of her, to dress her braided dark hair.
495.nuance: வந்தமாறே makes his coming the cause: the land's loneliness (புலம்பு) ends because he arrived, so the landscape stands for her and its comfort is hers.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains crashing and the millet in ear

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is spoken of in the third person to the woman, so the friend is the likely speaker

496.reading: The friend tells the woman of large lovely eyes that, with beasts sheltering in the bushes, the millet heavy in ear and the rains crashing and lashing, he who lived apart from her has come to be the companion of her shoulders; now let her hair of opening buds long for flowers again.
496.nuance: Hair that 'wants flowers' is hair that may be dressed again: a woman apart from her husband did not wear flowers, so the friend's last line is permission to adorn. The sense of மாமலி புலம்ப in line 2 is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: konrai in flower and termites swarming at the first rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is spoken of in the third person to the woman, so the friend is the likely speaker

497.reading: The friend tells the woman of noble bearing that the konrai flowers in many short garlands, the tall red anthills pour out winged termites, the beasts no longer go hungry and the rains have begun, because the war-loving lord has come thinking of her.
497.nuance: As in 495, the arrival is made the cause of the season (வந்த மாறே); the termites that the anthills 'offer' (பகர) are food that ends the beasts' hunger, so the plenty of the rains and the end of her want arrive together.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's war over, the waiting woman's body recovers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the woman's body is described with no pronoun and the man in the third person, so the friend likely speaks of her to the household

498.reading: Her shoulders have regained their beauty, her bangles stay in place and her long lined eyes have taken on a bright loveliness, because the king of the tusked elephants left off his war and the man of the hill country drove his swift tall chariot home.
498.nuance: The recovery is itemised in the order loss was itemised in the poems of separation: shoulders, bangles, eyes. The return depends on the king's release (வேந்து தொழில் விட்டென), not on the man's choice; and the hero is called வரையக நாடன், a man of the hills, in a mullai poem.

thinai_evidence.note: pidavam and thalavam in the rain-dressed forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is spoken of in the third person to the woman, so the friend is the likely speaker

499.reading: The friend tells the woman of sweet speech that our lover, thinking she would grieve greatly if she saw the forest dressed in the beauty of the rains, with pidavam blooming and thalavam in bud, did not stay away for his hard work but came, bringing back her fine beauty.
499.nuance: He reasons from what the season would do to her, not from his own longing: the forest is dangerous because she would see it. அருந்தொழிற்கு அகலாது says he left the hard task unfinished rather than miss the season.

thinai_evidence.note: konrai of the rains and the man back from the war camp

comparisons.tenor: the woman's eyes yellowed with pallor

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is addressed (நீ வந்த மாறே) and the woman spoken of as இவள், so the friend speaks to the returned man

500.reading: The friend tells the returned lord of strong horses, who lingered long in the wide camp of victorious war, that the kohl-lined eyes of this woman, gone yellow as konrai flowers, have regained their old beauty like the blue lilies of a long mountain pool, now that he has come.
500.nuance: The two flowers measure the change: the konrai, the rainy season's own yellow flower, gives the pallor, and the kuvalai of a hill pool, a kurinji thing, gives the restored eyes. Ending the decade by addressing him, the friend also reminds him how long the camp kept him (நீடிய).

links.note: Kar Narpathu's friend sees flowers bloom like the woman's eyes and hears them announce his return; in 492 the man sees peacock, mullai and deer as likenesses of her and comes home.
links.teaches: The same likening of the season's things to the woman works from both ends of the separation: for her the flowers that resemble her eyes are messengers of his return, while for him the creatures that resemble her are what sent him home, so the comparison is the bond that carries the promise across.

links.note: Akananuru 4's friend says the flowering land turns its back on loneliness (புலம்புபுறக் கொடுப்ப) as his chariot comes into view; 495's man says the scrub's loneliness has ended (புலம்பு தீர்ந்து) because he came.
links.teaches: What the friend in Akananuru offers as a sign that he is about to arrive, the man in 495 claims as his own doing, so the land's loneliness was read as the woman's own, ending at the same moment hers does.

links.note: Both have winged termites pouring from a red anthill (Purananuru: செம்புற்று ஈயல்; Ainkurunuru: நெடுஞ்செம் புற்றம் ஈயல்); Purananuru makes them the one-day life of kings who defied Vazhuthi.
links.teaches: The swarm of the first rains meant short-lived ruin in a war poem and food that ends the beasts' hunger in a love poem, and 497's war-loving lord stands between the two, come home from the kind of war in which other men were the termites.

links.note: In Akananuru 164 the man in the war camp says she would regain her old beauty in this season if only the king released him from his work (வேந்தன் வினைவிடப் பெறினே); 498 reports that the king left off his war (வேந்துதொழில் விட்டென) and her shoulders, bangles and eyes recovered.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems give the conditional and its fulfilment of one plot, and show that in these mullai returns the woman's beauty hung on the king's campaign, not on the husband's will alone.

links.note: The Kural's woman says the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only once she has seen him to her eyes' fill; 498 says her shoulders have regained their beauty because he came.
links.teaches: The Kural states as the woman's own condition that only his presence cures the pallor, and 498 shows that condition met and observed from outside, item by item on her body, so the couplet's claim is confirmed as the accepted course of the return.

links.note: The Kural's woman says he went away with his resolve as companion (உள்ளம் துணையாக) and she lives only by longing for his return; 496's friend says he has come back to be the companion of her shoulders (தோள் துணையாக).
links.teaches: The word துணை marks the turn of the plot: the reproach that he chose his resolve as companion over her is answered on his return, when the companionship is given back to her as embrace, so the Kural's complaint is a stage the akam story expects to close.

links.note: In 357 the man sees the season-dressed forest himself and gives up the journey for wealth; in 499 he gives up his hard work because she would grieve if she saw the rain-dressed forest.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru gives two reasons for the same turning back, the forest's beauty moving the man himself in the paalai decade and the forest's power to hurt her moving him in the mullai decade, so the season is at once his longing and his sense of her danger.

source_issues: 493 line 1: ஏறுமுதண் reads like a corruption of ஏறு முரண் (the bulls' contest); the sense of the line is taken that way and the verse marked uncertain.
494 line 4: திர்கினிப் is most likely தீர்கினிப் with the long vowel lost.
496 line 2: மாமலி புலம்ப is obscure in our text; the line is read only as the rains raging.
498 line 3: வேந்துகோட்டு யானை is probably ஏந்துகோட்டு யானை (elephant of lifted tusks), the வ repeated from the next வேந்து.
Decade title is printed as வரவுச் சிரப்புரைத்த பத்து; the usual spelling is சிறப்புரைத்த.
